headline: Controversy: Ishraque Hossain resigns as state minister to avoid party embarrassment
summary: The state minister for Liberation War affairs stepped down following backlash over an 'anti-drug drive' conducted with a firearm in hand.
details: Ishraque Hossain, the state minister for Liberation War affairs, announced his resignation on Monday afternoon at a press conference at the National Press Club.
The move comes amid controversy surrounding an 'anti-drug drive' he led, during which he was seen carrying a licensed firearm for his own safety.
Ishraque claimed that the media used images of the incident to push a specific agenda and expressed disappointment in how he was targeted.
He stated that after the backlash, he personally approached Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to request his resignation to prevent the BNP from being embarrassed.
Despite leaving the government, Ishraque announced that he will continue his campaign to eradicate drugs with the permission of the prime minister.
Ishraque is the eldest son of the late Sadeque Hossain Khoka, the former mayor of the undivided Dhaka City Corporation.
caption:

Ishraque claimed that the media used images of the incident to push a specific agenda and expressed disappointment in how he was targeted.

He stated that after the backlash, he personally approached Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to request his resignation to prevent the BNP from being embarrassed.

Despite leaving the government, Ishraque announced that he will continue his campaign to eradicate drugs with the permission of the prime minister.

Ishraque is the eldest son of the late Sadeque Hossain Khoka, the former mayor of the undivided Dhaka City Corporation.

headline_marked: New deal: [[Japan to recruit Bangladeshi workers]] from April 1
headline: New deal: Japan to recruit Bangladeshi workers from April 1
summary: A formal employment agreement has been signed, providing legal protections and new skill-development opportunities for Bangladeshi migrants in Japan.
details: Bangladesh and Japan have signed a new employment agreement, allowing the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in Japan starting from April 1 next year.
The Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development (ESDP-MOC) will be in effect for 10 years, with an initial 5-year term and an automatic 5-year extension.
The agreement was signed by the secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry and representatives from Japan's Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and other agencies.
Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury stated that the agreement ensures the highest possible level of protection for workers and strengthens bilateral cooperation.
Bangladeshi workers will receive legal protections equivalent to those enjoyed by local Japanese workers, including equal opportunities for men and women.
The agreement specifically protects female migrant workers, ensuring they do not face discrimination or dismissal due to pregnancy or childbirth.
The ministry noted that there is no mandatory provision to forcibly send workers back to Bangladesh if they become pregnant or give birth while working in Japan.
The two countries will formally exchange copies of the agreement during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's scheduled visit to Japan.
caption:
Japan opens its doors to Bangladeshi workers! A new 10-year agreement ensures legal protections and higher wages.

Bangladesh and Japan have signed a new employment agreement, allowing the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in Japan starting from April 1 next year.

The Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development (ESDP-MOC) will be in effect for 10 years, with an initial 5-year term and an automatic 5-year extension.

The agreement was signed by the secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry and representatives from Japan's Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and other agencies.

Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury stated that the agreement ensures the highest possible level of protection for workers and strengthens bilateral cooperation.

Bangladeshi workers will receive legal protections equivalent to those enjoyed by local Japanese workers, including equal opportunities for men and women.

The agreement specifically protects female migrant workers, ensuring they do not face discrimination or dismissal due to pregnancy or childbirth.

The ministry noted that there is no mandatory provision to forcibly send workers back to Bangladesh if they become pregnant or give birth while working in Japan.

The two countries will formally exchange copies of the agreement during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's scheduled visit to Japan.
